hello.title: Hello, Lua!
hello.summary: Write your first Lua program, print text and numbers, and calculate with the basic math operators.
hello.lesson.0: Lua is a small and fast programming language. Many games, apps and tools use it to run scripts. A Lua program is a text file whose name ends in `.lua`. You run it in a terminal with the command `lua hello.lua`.
hello.lesson.2: `print` is a **function**: a named piece of code that does a job. You call it with parentheses `()`. The value inside the parentheses is the **argument**. `print` writes it on the screen and then starts a new line.
hello.lesson.3: Text in quotes is a **string**. You can use double quotes `"` or single quotes `'`; both make the same string. Lua runs the lines of a program from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.6: Numbers have no quotes. Lua knows the operators `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). As in math, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses `()` decide what Lua calculates first.
hello.lesson.8: Lua has two kinds of numbers: **integers** are whole numbers such as `7`, and **floats** have a decimal point, such as `3.5`. The `/` operator always gives a float, even when the result is a whole number. `//` divides and rounds down to a whole number, `%` gives the remainder of a division, and `^` raises a number to a power.
hello.lesson.10: Look closely at the results: `6 / 2` prints `3.0`, not `3`. A float always shows a decimal point. `^` also always gives a float, so `2 ^ 3` is `8.0`.
hello.lesson.11: Two dashes `--` start a **comment**. Lua ignores everything from `--` to the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, like `-- 2`.
hello.card.0: `print("Hi")` writes a line on the screen
hello.card.3: `//` divides and rounds down, `%` is the remainder, `^` is a power
hello.card.4: `--` starts a comment; run a file with `lua file.lua`
hello-1.prompt: Which command runs the file hello.lua?
hello-1.explain: You start the Lua program `lua` and give it the name of the file to run.
hello-2.explain: `*` comes before `+`: first `4 * 2` is `8`, then `3 + 8` is `11`.
hello-3.explain: `/` always gives a float, so the result shows a decimal point: `3.0`.
hello-4.explain: `%` gives the remainder: `17` divided by `5` is `3` with the remainder `2`.
hello-5.explain: `//` divides and rounds down: `7 / 2` is `3.5`, rounded down `3`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hello, Lua!
hello-6.explain: `print` is the Lua function that writes a value on the screen.
hello-7.prompt: Match each operator with what it does.
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 2 times 5.
hello-8.explain: `*` multiplies. The calculation goes inside the parentheses of `print`.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Ready, Set and Go! on three lines.
hello-9.explain: Lua runs the lines from top to bottom, so the first line prints first.
hello-10.prompt: This program should print Hello, Lua and Bye on three lines. Which line has the bug?
hello-10.explain: The string `Lua` has no closing quote. Write `print("Lua")`.
hello-11.explain: `^` raises to a power and always gives a float: `2 ^ 2` is `4.0`.
hello-12.explain: Lua ignores the comment after `--`. The program prints `10`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in local variables, and meet the types number, string, boolean and nil and the type() function.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with the keyword `local`, a name, the equals sign `=` and a value. Here `=` means "store this value", not "is equal to". After that, the name stands for the value.
variables.lesson.2: You can give a variable a new value later. Write `local` only the first time; after that, use the name and `=`. Lua calculates the right side first, so `score = score + 5` adds `5` to the old value.
variables.lesson.4: Names may contain letters, digits and `_`, but they cannot start with a digit. Lua is **case-sensitive**: `age` and `Age` are two different variables. Some words, such as `local`, `end` and `if`, are **keywords** and cannot be names.
variables.lesson.5: Without `local`, you create a **global** variable that every part of the program can see and change. This causes mistakes that are hard to find. Always use `local` for new variables.
variables.lesson.6: You can create several variables in one line: `local a, b = 1, 2`. The first name gets the first value, the second name gets the second value.
variables.lesson.8: Every value has a **type**. The function `type()` returns the name of the type as a string. Integers and floats both have the type `number`, text has the type `string`, and the two values `true` and `false` have the type `boolean`.
variables.lesson.10: `nil` is a special value that means "no value". A variable that you create without a value is `nil`. The type of `nil` is also called `nil`.
variables.lesson.12: `tostring()` turns a value into a string, and `tonumber()` turns a string into a number. If the string does not contain a number, `tonumber()` returns `nil`.
variables.card.0: `local x = 5` creates a variable; `x = x + 1` changes it
variables.card.3: `nil` means no value; a new variable without a value is `nil`
variables-1.explain: `x` starts as `4`. Then `x = x + 3` stores `4 + 3`, which is `7`.
variables-2.explain: `"12"` is in quotes, so it is a string, even though it contains digits.
variables-3.statement: A variable that you create with `local x` and no value is `nil`.
variables-3.explain: A variable without a value holds `nil`, which means "no value".
variables-4.prompt: Complete the code so it creates a local variable.
variables-4.explain: Lua creates local variables with the keyword `local`. `var` and `let` come from other languages.
variables-5.explain: `local b = a` copies the value `5` into `b`. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.
variables-6.prompt: Match each value with its type.
variables-7.prompt: Build a line that creates a local variable total with the value 100.
variables-7.explain: First the keyword `local`, then the name, then `=` and the value.
variables-8.prompt: This program should print 15. Which line has the bug?
variables-8.explain: Lua is case-sensitive: `Tax` is not `tax`. `Tax` is `nil`, and you cannot add `nil`. Write `local total = price + tax`.
variables-9.explain: `"abc"` does not contain a number, so `tonumber()` returns `nil`.
variables-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 12.
variables-10.explain: `5 + 1` is `6`, and `6 * 2` is `12`. In the other order you get `5 * 2 + 1`, which is `11`.
variables-11.explain: `a` gets the first value `3` and `b` the second value `4`. `3 * 4` is `12`.
variables-12.explain: `Score` and `score` are two different variables. `print(Score)` prints `1`.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join strings with .., measure them with #, and change them with string.upper, string.sub, string.rep and string.format.
strings.lesson.0: The operator `..` (two dots) joins two strings into one. This is called **concatenation**. When you join a number with a string, Lua turns the number into text.
strings.lesson.2: Put `#` before a string to get its **length**: the number of characters. Spaces count too.
strings.lesson.4: `#` counts bytes, not letters. Letters such as `é` or `ü` take two bytes, so `#"é"` is `2`. With plain English letters, one letter is one byte.
strings.lesson.6: Lua keeps its string functions in the **string library**. You call them with `string`, a dot `.` and the name of the function. `string.upper(s)` returns `s` in capital letters, `string.lower(s)` in small letters, and `string.rep(s, n)` repeats `s` `n` times.
strings.lesson.8: These functions return a new string. They never change the original string, as the last line above shows. Store the result when you need it: `s = string.upper(s)`.
strings.lesson.9: `string.sub(s, i, j)` returns the part of `s` from position `i` to position `j`, both included. The first character has the position `1`. A negative position counts from the end: `-1` is the last character. Without `j`, the part goes to the end of the string.
strings.lesson.12: `string.format` builds a string from a pattern. In the pattern, `%s` stands for any value as text, `%d` for a whole number, and `%.2f` for a number with two digits after the decimal point. The values follow the pattern, in the same order.
strings.card.3: `string.sub(s, 2, 4)` takes characters 2 to 4; `-1` is the last one
strings.card.4: `string.format("%s has %d", name, n)`; `%.2f` shows two decimals
strings-1.explain: `..` joins the two strings without adding a space.
strings-2.explain: `#` gives the length: `banana` has six characters.
strings-3.explain: Positions start at `1`: position `2` is `e` and position `4` is `l`. Both ends are included.
strings-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints HELLO.
strings-4.explain: `string.upper` returns the string in capital letters.
strings-5.explain: `string.upper` returns a new string, but the program does not store it. `s` is still `lua`.
strings-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it gives.
strings-7.prompt: Build a line that prints the word three times.
strings-7.explain: `string.rep(word, 3)` repeats the word three times, and `print` writes the result.
strings-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Hi, Sam!
strings-8.explain: Each line uses the variable that the line before it creates.
strings-9.prompt: This program should print the first letter of the word. Which line has the bug?
strings-9.explain: In Lua, the first character has the position `1`, not `0`. Write `local first = string.sub(word, 1, 1)`.
strings-10.explain: Each `%d` is replaced by the next value: `2`, `3` and `2 + 3`, which is `5`.
strings-11.explain: `#s` is `3`. `..` joins the two numbers as text, so the result is `33`, not `6`.
strings-12.prompt: This program should print Price: 4.50. Which line has the bug?
strings-12.explain: `%d` only works with whole numbers, and `4.5` is not one. Write `string.format("Price: %.2f", price)`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, elseif and else, and combine conditions with and, or and not.
conditions.lesson.0: A **comparison** checks two values and gives a boolean: `true` or `false`. `==` means "is equal to", `~=` means "is not equal to", and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes. Remember: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs code only when a condition is true. Write `if`, the condition, `then`, the code and `end`. The code between `then` and `end` is a **block**. Indent it with 4 spaces so that it is easy to read.
conditions.lesson.4: `else` adds a block that runs when the condition is false. `elseif` checks another condition. Lua tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true. One `end` closes the whole `if`.
conditions.lesson.6: `elseif` is one word. `else if` with a space starts a new `if` inside the `else` block, and that `if` needs its own `end`.
conditions.lesson.8: `and` is true when both sides are true. `or` is true when at least one side is true. `not` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.
conditions.lesson.11: In a condition, only `false` and `nil` count as false. Every other value counts as true, also the number `0` and the empty string `""`.
conditions.lesson.13: `or` returns the first value that counts as true. So `name or "guest"` gives `name` when it has a value, and `"guest"` when `name` is `nil`. This is a common way to set a default value.
conditions.card.0: `if x > 0 then ... elseif x < 0 then ... else ... end`
conditions.card.3: Only `false` and `nil` count as false; `0` and `""` count as true
conditions-1.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, not `0`, so the condition is false and the `else` block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `~=` means "is not equal to". `3` is equal to `3`, so the result is `false`.
conditions-3.prompt: Complete the code so it prints not equal.
conditions-3.explain: Lua writes "is not equal to" as `~=`. Many other languages use `!=`, but Lua does not.
conditions-4.statement: In Lua, the number `0` counts as false in a condition.
conditions-4.explain: Only `false` and `nil` count as false. `0` counts as true.
conditions-5.explain: `15 > 25` is false, so Lua checks the `elseif`: `15 > 10` is true.
conditions-6.prompt: Match each operator with its meaning.
conditions-6.pairs.2: is less than or equal to
conditions-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints big.
conditions-7.explain: First create `n`. Then `if ... then` opens the block, the block prints, and `end` closes it.
conditions-8.prompt: This program should print adult for an age of 18 or more. Which line has the bug?
conditions-8.explain: After the condition, Lua needs the keyword `then`. Write `if age >= 18 then`.
conditions-9.explain: `name` is `nil`, which counts as false, so `or` gives the second value: `guest`.
conditions-10.prompt: Build the first line of an if that checks that x is greater than 0 and less than 10.
conditions-10.explain: `and` is true only when both comparisons are true. The condition goes between `if` and `then`.
conditions-11.explain: `nil` counts as false, and `not` turns it into `true`.
conditions-12.prompt: This program should print zero when n is 0. Which line has the bug?
conditions-12.explain: `=` stores a value; to compare, use `==`. Write `if n == 0 then`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with the numeric for loop, while and repeat ... until, and stop a loop early with break.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. The numeric `for` loop counts: `for i = 1, 5 do` sets `i` to `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` and `5`, one after the other, and runs the block between `do` and `end` once for each value. The end value is included.
loops.lesson.2: A third number sets the **step**: how much `i` changes each time. Without it, the step is `1`. A negative step counts down.
loops.lesson.4: Loops often build a result step by step. Create a variable before the loop and change it inside the loop. After the loop, the variable holds the result.
loops.lesson.6: The loop variable `i` is local to the loop: it only exists between `do` and `end`. Do not change it inside the loop; use another variable for your own values.
loops.lesson.8: A `while` loop repeats its block as long as its condition is true. Lua checks the condition before each round. Make sure the block changes something in the condition, or the loop never stops.
loops.lesson.10: `repeat ... until` checks the condition after each round, so the block always runs at least once. The loop stops as soon as the condition is true.
loops.lesson.12: `break` stops a loop at once. The program continues after the `end` of the loop.
loops.card.0: `for i = 1, 5 do ... end` counts from 1 to 5
loops.card.1: `for i = 10, 0, -2 do` counts down in steps of 2
loops.card.2: `while cond do ... end` checks before each round
loops.card.3: `repeat ... until cond` runs at least once
loops-2.prompt: How many times does this print Hi?
loops-2.explain: With the step `2`, `i` takes the values `2`, `4`, `6` and `8`. The end value is included.
loops-3.prompt: Complete the code so it counts down from 5 to 1.
loops-3.explain: To count down, the step must be negative. With the step `1`, the loop does not run at all.
loops-4.statement: A `repeat ... until` loop always runs its block at least once.
loops-4.explain: `repeat ... until` checks the condition after the block, so the block runs once before the first check.
loops-5.explain: `n` goes from `100` to `50`, `25`, `12` and `6`. `6 > 10` is false, so the loop stops.
loops-6.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 1, 2 and 3 on separate lines.
loops-6.explain: Print `i` first and then add `1`. In the other order, the program would print `2`, `3` and `4`.
loops-7.prompt: This program should print the numbers 1 to 5. Which line has the bug?
loops-7.explain: `i` gets smaller, so `i <= 5` stays true and the loop never stops. Write `i = i + 1`.
loops-8.prompt: Match each loop with what it does.
loops-9.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts 0, 5, 10.
loops-9.explain: Start value, end value, step: `for i = 0, 10, 5 do`.
loops-10.explain: `n` becomes `5`, `10` and `15`. Only `15 > 12` is true, so the loop stops there.
loops-11.explain: For `i = 4`, `4 * 3` is `12`, which is more than `10`, so `break` stops the loop. The last stored value is `3`.
loops-12.explain: The loop variable `i` only exists inside the loop. After `end`, `i` is an unknown name, so the program prints `nil`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions, return one or more values, accept any number of arguments and use functions as values.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. Write `local function`, a name, the **parameters** in parentheses, the block and `end`. Parameters are variables that get their values from the call. As with variables, `local` keeps the function local.
functions.lesson.2: `return` sends a value back to the caller. The call then stands for that value, so you can store it or use it in a calculation. Define a function before the line that calls it.
functions.lesson.4: When you pass fewer arguments than there are parameters, the missing parameters are `nil`. Together with `or`, this gives you default values.
functions.lesson.7: A function can return several values, separated by commas. To get them, write several variables on the left side of `=`.
functions.lesson.9: Three dots `...` as the last parameter accept any number of arguments. `select("#", ...)` gives the number of arguments, and `select(i, ...)` gives the argument at position `i`.
functions.lesson.12: A function is a value, like a number or a string. You can store it in a variable and pass it to another function. `function(x) ... end` without a name creates an **anonymous function**.
functions.card.0: `local function add(a, b) return a + b end`
functions.card.2: `return a, b` returns two values: `local x, y = f()`
functions.card.3: `...` accepts any number of arguments; `select("#", ...)` counts them
functions.card.4: Functions are values: `local f = function(x) return x * 2 end`
functions-2.explain: The call passes no argument, so the parameter `x` is `nil`, and `print` writes `nil`.
functions-3.prompt: Complete the function so it gives back the doubled number.
functions-3.explain: `return` sends the value back to the caller, so `print` gets `8`.
functions-4.explain: `pair()` returns two values: `a` gets `1` and `b` gets `2`. `1 + 2` is `3`.
functions-5.explain: The function returns `3 + 4` and `3 * 4`. `p` gets the second value, `12`.
functions-6.prompt: This program should print 25. Which line has the bug?
functions-6.explain: A calculation alone is not a statement. The function must send the result back: `return n * n`.
functions-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 9.
functions-7.explain: Define the function first, from `local function` to `end`. Then call it.
functions-8.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
functions-9.prompt: Build the first line of a local function named add with the parameters a and b.
functions-9.explain: `local function`, then the name and the parameters in parentheses.
functions-10.explain: `select("#", ...)` counts the arguments: `"a"`, `"b"` and `"c"` are three.
functions-12.prompt: This program should print Hi, Max. Which line has the bug?
functions-12.explain: Without quotes, `Max` is a variable name, and that variable is `nil`. Write `greet("Max")`.
tables.title: Tables as lists
tables.summary: Keep many values in one table: read them by position, count them with #, loop with ipairs, and add, remove and join items.
tables.lesson.0: A **table** holds many values. It is the only data structure in Lua. Write the values between braces `{}`, separated by commas. A table like this is a **list**: each value has a position, called its **index**.
tables.lesson.2: In Lua, the first index is `1`, not `0` as in many other languages. `t[i]` reads the value at index `i`, `#t` gives the length of the list, and `t[i] = v` changes a value. An index without a value gives `nil`.
tables.lesson.5: A numeric `for` loop from `1` to `#t` visits every index. Shorter is `ipairs`: `for i, v in ipairs(t) do` gives you the index `i` and the value `v` of each item, in order.
tables.lesson.7: When you do not need the index, call it `_`: `for _, v in ipairs(t) do`. `_` is a normal variable name, but it tells readers that the value is not used.
tables.lesson.9: `table.insert(t, v)` adds `v` at the end of the list. `table.insert(t, 1, v)` adds it at index `1` and moves the other items up. `table.remove(t)` removes the last item and returns it.
tables.lesson.11: `table.concat(t, sep)` joins all items of a list into one string, with `sep` between them. The items must be strings or numbers.
tables.lesson.13: `print(t)` does not show the items of a table. It prints the word `table` and a memory address, which changes from run to run. Use `table.concat` or a loop to see the items.
tables.card.1: `#t` is the length; `t[#t]` is the last item
tables.card.2: `for i, v in ipairs(t) do ... end`
tables.card.4: `table.concat(t, ", ")` joins the items into a string
tables-1.explain: The first index is `1`, so `t[2]` is the second item: `10`.
tables-2.explain: `#t` gives the number of items in the list: four.
tables-3.statement: In Lua, the first item of a list has the index `0`.
tables-3.explain: Lua lists start at index `1`. `t[0]` is `nil` in a list that you create with braces.
tables-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints every name.
tables-4.explain: `ipairs` gives the index and the value of each item, in order.
tables-5.explain: `x` and `y` are added at the end. Then `z` goes to index `1`, and the others move up.
tables-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with what it does.
tables-6.pairs.2: adds an item at the end
tables-6.pairs.4: joins the items into a string
tables-7.prompt: Build a line that adds "milk" at the end of the list.
tables-7.explain: `table.insert` takes the list first and then the new value.
tables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 60.
tables-8.explain: `total` starts with the first price, and the loop adds the prices at the indexes `2` and `3`.
tables-9.prompt: This program should print the last fruit. Which line has the bug?
tables-9.explain: `#fruits` is `3`, the index of the last item. Index `4` has no value. Write `fruits[#fruits]`.
tables-10.explain: `table.remove` returns the last item, `3`, and the list keeps two items. `3 + 2` is `5`.
tables-11.explain: The loop adds index times value: `1 * 4 + 2 * 5 + 3 * 6` is `4 + 10 + 18`, which is `32`.
tables-12.prompt: This program should print a, b, c. Which line has the bug?
tables-12.explain: `table.insert` needs the list first and the value second. Write `table.insert(letters, "c")`.
objects.title: Tables as dictionaries and objects
objects.summary: Store values under keys, loop over them with pairs, put tables inside tables, and give tables their own methods with a colon.
objects.lesson.0: A table can also store values under names, called **keys**. Write `key = value` inside the braces. You read a value with a dot, `t.key`, or with brackets and a string, `t["key"]`. A table like this works as a **dictionary**.
objects.lesson.2: Assign a value to a key to add or change it. Assign `nil` to remove the key. Brackets also work with a key in a variable: `t[k]`.
objects.lesson.4: `#t` only counts list items, which have the indexes `1`, `2`, `3` and so on. For a table with keys such as `name`, `#t` gives `0`.
objects.lesson.6: `pairs(t)` visits every key and its value: `for key, value in pairs(t) do`. The order is not defined, and it can differ from the order in your code. Use `pairs` when the order does not matter, for example for a sum or a count.
objects.lesson.8: A value in a table can be another table. This lets you describe structured data, for example a game character with a position and a list of items. Chain dots and brackets to reach the inner values.
objects.lesson.11: A function stored in a table is a **method**. Write `function account:deposit(n)` with a colon `:` to create one. Inside the method, `self` is the table that the method belongs to. Call it with a colon too: `account:deposit(50)` is short for `account.deposit(account, 50)`.
objects.lesson.13: Strings have methods too: `s:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(s)`, and `s:sub(1, 3)` is the same as `string.sub(s, 1, 3)`.
objects.card.1: `p.name` or `p["name"]` reads a value; `p.age = nil` removes it
objects.card.2: `for k, v in pairs(t) do ... end` visits all keys, in no fixed order
objects-2.explain: `t["b"]` is the same as `t.b`: the value stored under the key `b`.
objects-3.statement: `pairs` always visits the keys in the order in which you wrote them.
objects-3.explain: The order of `pairs` is not defined. Use it only when the order does not matter.
objects-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Ana.
objects-4.explain: A dot reads the value under a key: `user.name`. The colon is for calling methods.
objects-5.explain: `p.x` becomes `1 + 4`, which is `5`. Then the new key `y` gets `5 * 2`, which is `10`.
objects-6.prompt: Match each piece of code with its meaning.
objects-7.prompt: Build a line that calls the method greet of the table bot.
objects-7.explain: A colon calls the method and passes `bot` as `self`.
objects-8.prompt: This program should print 15. Which line has the bug?
objects-8.explain: With a dot, `5` becomes `self` and `n` is `nil`. Call the method with a colon: `counter:add(5)`.
objects-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Hi, I am Lia.
objects-9.explain: Create the table first, then add the method to it, and call the method at the end.
objects-10.explain: `box.size` is the inner table. `box.size.w` is `2` and `box.size.h` is `3`, and `2 * 3` is `6`.
objects-11.explain: `word:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(word)`. Then `..` adds the `!`.
objects-12.explain: The loop visits all three values in some order. Only `5` and `7` are greater than `2`, so `n` is `2` in any order.
